utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, everybody. Out of an abundance of caution, may I request that we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I just would note two things. The first with respect to timing is that, as we understand it, after this witness finishes, we've been told about the next eight witnesses that are coming, and of those eight witnesses, four of them we have been told will testify pursuant to 92 ter, which is the old 89(F). It's -- it is, to be fair, the last four of the eight, as I understand it. And of those four, there has been a motion filed with respect to one, which the Court referenced, and we have also received a statement - and I put "statement" in quotation marks for the moment, and I'll explain that in a moment - of another of the four. And I had understood that the Defence was going to file the motion with respect to that other one yesterday but I'm not sure if that's been done. But that leaves two outstanding in the next batch of eight and -- that we have not received any kind of statement for, and there is an urgency to get those statements because we need to prepare the cross-examinations of those witnesses, particularly since these four are going to be one after another, so it's going to be one cross-examination after another. So obviously we will have to prepare ahead of time for that because we'll have not a lot of time between witnesses to prepare. So just to underline that point that we do need those statements. The second point, the second thing I wanted to say, and we were actually intending to file something written with the Trial Chamber about this tomorrow and we may still do so, is the -- we have been talking about witness statements and the rule, 92 ter, talks about witness statements, which I understand to mean in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal generally to mean a signed statement by the witness. What was attached to the motion filed I believe Friday with respect to the one witness that Your Honour referred to was not what I would call a witness statement. It was not signed, there was no indication of the circumstances of how the statement -- the information was taken, was there an interview, was it written by the witness, there was none of that information, and that does cause us a little bit after concern. It's just a long summary. And I think we are entitled and the rule contemplates that we be provided a written -- a signed statement of the witness with information about how that statement was taken. Otherwise, it leaves us very much in the dark about who wrote that statement and under what circumstances and how it came to be. Fine, the witness comes into court and says, "Yes, this is what I would say," but I think we need to know more than that about how the statement was generated before we can deal with that witness. So it seems to me that right from the start, when these statements are provided to us, when they are filed, that information should be included and they should be signed statements, and we should also receive the B/C/S version of the statement, which I assume is the original. We are getting these translations but not the B/C/S original. Whatever that is, whether it was written by -- and we've heard various ways that these statements have come into being, sometimes written by the witness themselves, sometimes an interview by the investigator. So I would make that point, and I don't know if it's necessary, now that we've said it, to file something on it tomorrow, in response to the first motion. I also have another issue, a very brief issue to raise that's completely unrelated, but I won't do that until we are finished with this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, barring the point that you are making about the statement being a signed statement, I'm not sure whether you would like to hear Mr. Milovancevic once more on when and how and -- when he hopes to file these documents. I think he has made his point.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. I have no need for that, Your Honour. I've understood what Mr. Milovancevic has said and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right. Or we can raise with him, Mr. Milovancevic, apparently your 92 bis statement has to be a statement that's signed by the witness or the witness statements must be statements that are signed by the witness. And apparently you're supposed also to give the original B/C/S version. I haven't sort of studied the rule sufficiently to be able to say yes, that's the position, or no, that's not the position. But I don't know whether you do have any comment strictly on just those two points, the B/C/S version and a signed statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, permit me to do this after the break, after I've consulted with my team. Statements in B/C/S exist. I understood the question and I understand what my learned friend is after. But let me consult with my team colleagues and let us do this after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure what it is you want to consult with. All I want to find out from you, do you accept that indeed you owe your learned friend a B/C/S version and that you owe him a signed statement, and if you do accept those you've just got to tell us whether you think you can provide those without having to consult during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour, this is -- this I take as normal to have a B/C/S statement and a translation into English and for that statement to be signed. But let me consult with the Defence team on how this is done so that I'll be in a position more precisely to tell you when and how we are going to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. We will hear from you after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, and there was a third thing with respect to the statements and that is the circumstances under which they were taken, were they -- was it an interview, was it a -- did the witness write the statement himself, that kind of information I think is something that should be included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You hear that, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have heard Your Honour. We interviewed all these witnesses. Maybe we have provided them with information, and of course we are going to report to the learned colleague about these circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are we done with housekeeping issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, just one more brief one which is on an unrelated issue. We received today a motion with respect to safe conduct of several witnesses. The motion was filed confidentially, so I won't refer even the numbers of the witnesses just out of an abundance of caution. But what concerned us about this motion, and as Your Honours know, we have taken the position that we will not oppose these motions as a matter of course. However, there was something that stood out in this motion that caused us concern which is there is an ex parte annex which provides information about the witnesses. According to a footnote, it contains personal information about the witnesses and that's all that it says. It's not clear to us why that should be filed ex parte and on the face of it, we think we should receive that annex filed confidential, fine, but I don't see any basis in the motion for why it should be ex parte and why we should not be permitted to see it. That's the only issue I wanted to press. Perhaps there is a reason but it has not been made apparent to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I personally haven't seen that motion. Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that we respond after the first break with regard to this question as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. Are you happy with that, Mr. Whiting? Thank you very much. Is that it, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Any housekeeping, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at this point, no. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next -- we can call the witness in. I think also the witness comes in under private session conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. May I remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. Is that understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Where are we? It's still with you, Mr. Milovancevic. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, good afternoon. The Defence hopes that we will complete your examination-in-chief during this session. Please keep in mind our joint obligation to pause between question and answer for the sake of the interpreters and please also bear in mind the protective measures which have been established. And in the event you need to refer to any functions that you performed or posts that you held, please indicate that so that we could move into private session and I will of course on my part bear that in mind. Thank you. On Friday, as one of the last questions, we dealt with the topic of negotiations on the possible -- on a possible cease-fire after an attack by Croatian armed forces and units on the protected zone, the protected United Nations zone in Western Slavonia. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You described that on the first day, the 1st of May, the negotiations fell through, that you returned to Knin on the 2nd of May, early on the 2nd of May by helicopter, and that in the afternoon on the 2nd of May an offer for a cease-fire was brought by international intermediaries, that that offer was accepted by the leadership of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and that in the afternoon on the 3rd of May the Croatian side as well accepted that cessation of hostilities agreement. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: As a participant in these talks on a cessation of hostilities, can you tell us what information you have, what you know, about whether United Nations forces, the UNPROFOR, the civilian police of the United Nations, Mr. Akashi and other representatives of the international community, whether they were aware of the sufferings of the civilian Serbs in Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: They had to be aware of the suffering of the population, of that population, because they had their observers and forces in the territory of Western Slavonia. Also, in later talks they pointed out that there had been sufferings and that they were endeavouring to take proper care of the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: In these negotiations, did the Serbian side inform the international community about the sufferings of the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes. It was pointed out that large numbers of civilians have been killed, that they were encircled and that they needed help. It was also stressed that the -- that the Croatian forces, after the massacre of the population of civilians in -- on the road, actually cleansed the highway using water tank trucks of blood and every other trace of that crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the activities of the Croatian army and police in the area lasted for sometime after that, also after the agreement, if I understood you correctly. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether anyone from the Croatian side, as far as you know, had been indicted -- has been indicted because of the suffering of the civilians, because of the massacres that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I object on the grounds of relevance. I don't think this is relevant to our trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic? Relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The highest possible relevance, Your Honours. The highest possible. Because the Prosecution claims in the indictment that operations in Western Slavonia by Croatian armed forces lasted only for one day, and that Mr. Martic acted in retaliation. The Croatian side, the Croatian president, the expert who featured in this proceeding, actually said that according to them there had been at least 168 civilians killed, and therefore we are interested in hearing what the criteria are for treating this particular issue, and what is the reason for only Mr. Martic's being -- Martic being in the docket. And I should like to be given also a reply to another question in that connection: What objective in mind is this being done in this way? By this question, I'm actually preparing the ground for a document which we propose to introduce subsequently through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Simply that nothing that counsel has said talks about the relevance to this trial. This is not the first time that we go down this road, Your Honour. Defence counsel wants to change the focus of trial away from whether or not Milan Martic is responsible for the crimes alleged in the indictment to whether someone else is responsible for some other crimes. And those are issues which my colleagues in the office deal with in other cases, and there are other cases here in which those might be relevant, but this case is about Milan Martic and his responsibility for what's alleged in the indictment. By the way, the indictment does not say that Operation Flash only lasted on one day. It says on the 1st of May, the Croatian army launched an attack against Western Slavonia. It doesn't say in any, shape, or form that it lasted only one day, so counsel is wrong on the specifics and I think wrong also on the issue of relevance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the question is irrelevant. It's ruled out of order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you take your decision, but I should like to say something to respond to what my colleague has said, but as you have taken your decision, I will not insist that the Chamber decide on this issue and I shall proceed with my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What is your attitude, Mr. Witness, what is your position? You held posts which enable you to give an answer to this question. Can one at all accept the argument that there had been no proof of heinous crimes in Western Slavonia. Observed from your aspect, this is something that you should know. Can one say that there were no -- there was no proof?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: No. One cannot say that. There was plenty of proof, and the proof was also carried in the mass media and shown on television. And when it was not only the Serbian side that showed them but also members -- representatives of the Helsinki board as well as -- Helsinki Committee as well as Croatian media also showed those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this treatment of crimes in Western Slavonia -- actually, does this attitude to such crimes point to the position of a part of the international community vis-a-vis events on a part of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and the Serbian population in that area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: It certainly does. The international community --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting the witness. I again object on the grounds of relevance. I don't see what this has to do with this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I have a problem that when the Court has ruled that a question is out of order, it becomes absolutely disingenuous of counsel to reintroduce the same question in different words. It's exactly the same point. And to prefix it by the witness's attitude before you put the question doesn't change the nature of the question. It's still the same question. This question is not relevant to these proceedings. If you want to know why Croats are not being charged, if they are not being charged, I don't know, I don't control the cases, I think you must then go to the main office of the OTP and find out from them why they are not charging Croats. Here we are not dealing with the charge against Croats. We are dealing with the charge against not even Serbians but against one person, Milan Martic. Now, atrocities that were committed by Croats will be charged in cases that are dealing with those Croats here. And I think you've got to bear in mind that here in this trial we are not looking at what Croats did but we are looking at what Milan Martic did. And ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me. With all due respect, allow me to present a position which is different to yours, Your Honour, Judge Moloto. You decided -- you made a decision regarding my question, whether the witness knew whether there had been any trials. But now I'm discussing a much wider topic; that is, the attitude of a part of the international community towards the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and the Serbian population, a question of their political position to them which is reflected and can be manifested in different ways, which is the topic that I intend to deal with right now with the witness, because he actually participated in the negotiations with the people concerned. The international community thus can be right and then again it can be wrong. What I'm trying to elicit from the witness is a position on that. What was, what is the position of the international community towards a specific issue. That position of the international community is something that I'm logically interested in because one of the key topics that we dealt with was the Vance Plan and its implementation. The Defence is very much interested in whether the international community is implementing consistently the Vance Plan or is it in breach of it. So this is the line of questioning that I'm pursuing. I have eliminated the question that you ruled on. I'm asking about the attitude of the international community which can be manifested in different ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure I understand that response. It seems to be that it may be an argument we hear from the Defence in other submissions, such as the military expert report that was filed recently, that it's not the Serbs who are to blame, it's the international community that's to blame for events there. I don't think that is relevant to this trial. Frankly, I maintain my objection, Your Honour. I don't understand the response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Black, is Defence counsel making a challenge in respect of the credibility of members of the international community? And statements made in the course of the trial as to a particular state of affairs, and he's hoping to challenge the accuracy of the state of affairs by seeking to undermine the credit of those members of the international community. This is how I understand it. Now, whether that is something that he's entitled to do, I think I'd probably have to hear him further to be convinced that this is the right way to go about it. And I do agree that it could effectively be dealt with in address, because he has actually got the state of affairs as known to his witness, as I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. I hear what you say, Judge. My only problem is that how do you undermine the credibility of the international community here? How do you do that? Is that really part of their case? Obviously, through his own witnesses, he knows he can tell us what happened and as you rightly say in an address he can say, "This is what happened, this is what the international community did, and therefore we think they were not fair." But they are not on trial, the international community. This is my problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I think probably part of the difficulty is that Mr. Milovancevic has not been specific and has not said in respect of X witness, Y witness, Z witness, such and such has been said, do you agree with that position and if not, why not? Which is a bit different. But to put it in that general term I think is part of what is creating the problem in the attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the problem. That's the problem. And I don't know how this -- how following this point of -- this line of questioning advances the case of Mr. Martic or undermines the case of the Prosecution. I really don't know how it does that, particularly because we still don't know Mr. Milovancevic's theory of this case. We've asked this from the beginning. He has refused to tell us. We don't know what his theory of the case is. And it becomes very difficult to determine questions of relevance when you don't know the Defence's theory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can give you much more direct answer than the one that I'm going to give but I'm risking tampering with the witness, influencing the witness, but I will say the following because the witness is present.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, if the witness needs to be excused for -- rather than say something that would risk influencing the witness I think we should excuse the witness, if necessary, if it can't be said in a way that doesn't carry that risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you prefer that, Mr. Milovancevic? Would you prefer that we excuse the witness so that you can explain your point clearly? Because we really don't understand you, you know, and I think for the Chamber to be able to rule on your -- on the objection, the Chamber must understand exactly what your position is. And I think the Chamber might as well order that the witness be excused for a couple of minutes. We'll call him when we are ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just about to propose that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome, Mr. Milovancevic. Thanks for the thought.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess we were in private session for purposes of excusing the witness. Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic, just tell us exactly what your point is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I shall endeavour to be as brief as possible. The basic thesis of the Defence is that the international community is the chief provoker of the war in Yugoslavia, that it actually instigated a war, that it conducted that war and controlled that war. The only joint criminal enterprise which exists exists on the part of the Republics of Croatia and Slovenia which waged, started a secessionist war in order to gain independence and to secede from Yugoslavia. In that light, the behaviour of the representatives of the international community is of direct bearing on the events that the witness is talking about. The witness talked about the operations in Miljevacki plateau and Maslenica and he's now talking about a third one, Operation Flash, and there have been no sanctions whatsoever for those who did those on the part of the international community. What are we talking about, Your Honours, are these double standards. These are the answers that I'm seeking. When I say the international community, I'm speaking about influential countries which were influential in that particular point of time in that particular area. And there are a number of relevant documents that we talked about and which we challenge because reports to the United Nations Security Council is not evidence, is not proof. It is just a submission, an analysis, an estimate, of the situation in the field which may or may not be correct. Whether the international community sent truthful reports from the field is something that needs to be examined. This witness also spoke about that. Mr. McElligott and his report about the suffering of the Croatian population in the period from August 1992 to May 1993 said in his report that these were untruthful claims. This is what I'm talking about. What happened in Western Slavonia is also an indicator of such practices. The very fact that there is no persecution -- sorry, prosecution today of such persons is actually indication of the position of the international community in respect of those events. How is it possible that Mr. Martic has been indicted for five people killed in Zagreb whereas the other side killed 176 persons in the operations in question? How is this possible? Is this a double standard, double criterion? And we have documents corroborating that. That is why I said all this. Of course, I cannot say there in front of the witness and I can be said to be asking him a leading question, if I did that. But I do wish to introduce some documents along this line of questioning through this witness very shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, if you say you're going to be brief, please try to be brief. Let me ask you just one question. Do you want these influential international countries that you refer to to be tried? Is that what you're saying? You would like those countries to be tried? You haven't mentioned them by name but you talked of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much for your -- for this question. I'm not the International Tribunal's Prosecutor. This is not my purpose. I am defending Mr. Martic but I'm demonstrating that the political attitude of certain countries may have resulted --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: There is a question I'd like to ask you and I'd like to get down to the nitty-gritty, so to speak, with you: Mr. Milovancevic, had the powers that be that you claim should have been charged, let's take it academically and hypothetically that they had been charged, as we stand here today, then what would your response be? How would it affect your case? How would it affect the case for the Prosecution had those persons in the international community that you say are the provocateurs, how would it affect the Prosecution's case and your case and the issues that this Honourable Trial Chamber has to decide, those issue that is we have to decide? That's what I want to hear from you because I do not comprehend.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. Had those representatives of the leading elites who brought about war in the former Yugoslavia been in the dock, I'm sure that Mr. Martic would not have spent four and a half years here. He would have been a free man because he's an innocent man, and this is what we are trying to prove. When we talk about the role of the international community, I'm talking about support to illegal secession which is the plague of the international order. The right to self-determination pursuant to UN documents is not contentious, but to enforce that by arms runs counter to international order, international law. Croatian leadership committed this war against peace and enjoyed the support of certain international factors. And this is what I'm saying and we are trying to demonstrate that, and Mr. Martic and his people are a victim in all this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, I still don't understand your argument. Now, you say if those people were charged hypothetically, Mr. Martic would be walking a free man. You said a little earlier, Mr. Martic is being charged for killing five people in Zagreb, other people have killed 160.000 people or whatever number you gave. Are you saying that if those people had been charged with killing those 160,000 people, Mr. Martic would then have to walk free for having killed the five?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Martic did not kill five people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is what you said earlier. You said Mr. Martic is being charged for killing five people in Zagreb. I'm saying --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the killing of them. This is the distinction, because of the death of five civilians in Zagreb, and this is not questioned at a moment when the military of the Republic of Serbian Krajina conducted legitimate defence and at a point when international community was mute, UN protected area is being attacked and the UN was silent. When this happened in Bosnia the whole of the Republika Srpska was bombed, Your Honour. I wonder whether it went -- was done this way because Serbs had to be bombed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me tell you one thing, Mr. Milovancevic, and I think I would like to close this discussion because I think it's taken far too much than it is worth. As you've rightly referred to the international community and the United Nations and the perhaps even this Tribunal as an agent of the United Nations, is a much bigger organisation than the three of us sitting here. We have been allocated one case, Mr. Martic's case. We are not here to adjudicate on other cases that are not before us, cases of international countries, of international communities. We are here to adjudicate one case. And the questions that you are directing at why so and so has not been charged and so and so has been charged, those are political questions that you must ask the powers that be who have decided what should be done and what shouldn't be done. We can only deal here with one case at a time. If after Mr. Martic's case this court is given a case to charge an international person, we will do so. And I just want to say to you that what goes to the charge against those people has nothing to do with what goes to the charges against Mr. Martic, and we would like to deal with Mr. Martic's case here and now. Okay? I'm going to give you three sentences to say and then [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree with what you said. I'm not saying that -- whether other people should have been indicted or not. We are discussing whether this Honourable Chamber is given a chance to get informed of the realistic real situation, military, political, in the field so that they may conclude what were the circumstances for certain developments and events, and this is what my presentation goes for. I'm not discussing whether you are trying this case. I'm talking about certain other issues. Some witnesses have been introduced, some materials were led, which in my opinion, in our opinion, run counter to the realistic situation in the field, and which reflect a double standard and different attitude towards the two sides in the conflict. If there is a possibility for us to lead this information before you so that you may conclude whether things were this way as presented by the Prosecutor or in another manner, we are not dealing with charging the international community. And this has gone far beyond what Honourable Judge Nosworthy spoke about. When I discussed about this, what would have happened had somebody else been indicted, that's a hypothetical question, but it was in the context of determining the general political, international, diplomatic and military circumstances, and this is what I wanted to point out to the Chamber. We've read many UN resolutions, documents, reports, as evidence, and I believe it is possible -- it is necessary to judge their objectivity. I'm not saying, and I cannot say, and I don't have the facts that the whole of the UN has been inclined in this way but we do have some documents and would like to lead them for you to make your conclusions about them. And I am sorry that I took more than three sentences as instructed by you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You need to do that to the extent that what you do is relevant to Mr. Martic's case, Mr. Milovancevic, and if it is not relevant, I'm afraid we cannot allow that. You see, you keep talking of double standards, double standards on whose part I don't know, and I'm not even in a position to answer the question of double standards because what you are talking about is just not before me. All I want are facts related to the charges against Mr. Martic and I would like you to tell me something that advances Mr. Martic's case or undermines the Prosecution's case against Mr. Martic. Those are the two things that will determine to a very large extent any relevance of what you may bring about, and if what you bring about doesn't bear on either of those two issues, then it doesn't become relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully accept what you're saying, with one remark. The witness that was excused spoke that as a person involved in a certain profession, had contacts with the civilian police and that's out on the ground, he was told one thing and then to his astonishment he read completely different reports that were sent to the UN Security Council. So one question in context with the UN representatives in one way which is favourable to the Serbs and then a report comes to the UN which is completely different, and this is what I'm focusing on, which reflects the position of the accused. This is what I'm trying to do. I'm trying to link the defendant's position with that situation, and in this context, I am mentioning double standards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just ask the witness exactly what he knows about what happened. Put that on the record. And then you can compare it with any report that you want to compare it with, you know, rather than go the way you were going. I think if you ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I would also regard that very necessary, Mr. Milovancevic, that you are more precise in such questions and abstain from any generalisations of the so-called international community, also saying parts of this same international community. That is really not possible to work in this way to ask questions like the one you asked when the debate now then came up. This was: Was this treatment of crimes in Western Slavonia actually -- does this attitude to such crimes -- there is no English but this is what the transcript says, does this attitude to such crimes point to the position of a part of the international community vis-a-vis events on a part of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina and the Serbian population in that area? That is impossible to answer such a question. It's not a question of a political -- of a criminal procedure but rather of a political discussion or debate. So please abstain from such questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just elicit facts from this witness, Mr. Milovancevic, and all what we are saying in that sentence which Judge has just referred to, you can keep it for argument. You can then say, "I asked these questions, these were the answers, this is what the reports say, I therefore submit that the international community exercised double standards. You can do that at the time of argument. Shall we call the witness? May the witness be brought in. Just for the record, the question as formulated earlier is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the witness is brought back, maybe this is an opportunity for me to bring to your attention that my learned colleague Black when asking the question that the international community had accepted the intervention that we are discussing because of the non-enforcement of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to continue with my questioning. I will ask you a different question. You attended or you said that you attended many meetings with the representatives of the UNCIVPOL, that you attended such meetings on a monthly basis to discuss contentious issues, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What was the estimate and assessment of UNCIVPOL representatives of the attitude of the MUP of Krajina towards the UNCIVPOL and the tasks out in the field?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: UNCIVPOL representatives an at such meetings expressed their gratitude for the work of the organs of the interior of RSK in such difficult circumstances. They also said that they were satisfied with the cooperation and that there were certain incidents, maybe crimes, that had to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You saw a UN document about crimes against the Croats in the south sector in August 1992, May 1993 period.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Such a report submitted by a civilian police officer reflect what was going on on the ground and what you discussed with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is enough. Please, Mr. Usher, I would like you to distribute a document of the Defence to the Chamber and the OTP. This is the document that we submitted to the other party and the Chamber on Friday, but partially translated. I believe that there are enough copies for the interpreters as well. This document is in B/C/S. It is minutes of a meeting of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Mr. Martic, with the deputy commander of UN forces, Cedric Thornberry, which -- it is submitted in the B/C/S version and there is a translation attached to it. Sir, this reflects the minutes of that meeting. We translated in such a way as to -- as for the pages in B/C/S and English match to -- for easier referencing. Witness, can you see that minutes are dated 14th of June, 1993, and under 1 and 2, does it state that Milan Martic, Minister of the Interior of RSK, is present, and under 2, Cedric Thornberry, deputy of the UN forces commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under 6, does it state that Sankovic, Milenko, Chief of Staff of the Ministry of the Interior and the minutes taker is also present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to take a look at the last page of the document, page 9. It states the hour when the meeting was concluded and who took the minutes and it was -- it is signed. Can you read for us who took the minutes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Milenko Sankovic kept the minutes and this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When you say that this is his signature, are you saying that you know this person and that you know what his signature looks like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now please take a look at page 3 of these minutes. In the B/C/S and in the English, it is page 3. In the middle of the page, the words of Mr. Thornberry are quoted, and he says: "I have a question. Do you have any comments or objections regarding the work of the civilian police?" Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under that, Mr. Martic's reply: "Not for the time being, except that for -- that earlier, they took unto themselves the right to conduct autonomous investigations without consulting us. We aspire to have the rule of law, and it is not our intention to hide any crimes. You know that the proceedings are being instigated and are being conducted against those who have perpetrated crimes." Do you see that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Now we have Mr. Thornberry's response to these words who says in the next paragraph: "I asked this because our chief of police answers directly personally to me. And they told me that we -- you have very good cooperation. That they had very good cooperation. They told me that your people respected the civilian police and not the military police. I'm surprised about what you said about France and Germany. I don't know what they are doing. It surprised me that they are offering suicidal advice to Croatia." Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Thornberry says, "I ask this because our chief of police answers directly to me," what chief of police is he referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: He's referring to the chief of the CIVPOL, of the civilian police. I don't know who was that person at that particular point in time but that is whom he means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Cedric Thornberry, the deputy UN force commander informs Mr. Martic here that the civilian police chief was directly answerable to him and that he had been told that the cooperation was very good. Did I understand this text well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes. That is exactly what I've been saying all the time, that in contacts with us, in meetings with us, civilian police representatives expressed their gratitude to us for the activities that we were undertaking in such complex circumstances which were a state of neither war or peace. Very, very complicated situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Under this we have Mr. Martic's words, in reference to Mr. Thornberry's comment on Germany and France. Mr. Martic says: "You said that Croatia would not attack us on the 22nd of January (1993)."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a copy of the text. This is a translation from the booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, do you have a spare copy for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, when did this document come to your attention?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Nosworthy, this document was in the possession of the witness present here and the witness actually brought this document with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: But Mr. Thornberry has not been confronted with the contents of this document when he was here in the witness box.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Thornberry was not here. Probably confused him with Mr. Kirudja, this other person. Mr. Thornberry was not a witness in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my apologies. I stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall just -- I shall just ask another question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Martic responds to Mr. Thornberry and said: "You talked like this, that Croatia would not attack us on the 21st and 22nd of January, 1993 ... "I'm surprised that you don't know for Germany's and France's approval given to Croatia for attack." Is this correct, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go to page 4 of the document. What did Mr. Thornberry have to say to that. So we are talking about the deputy commander of the UN force commander, of the peace forces of the UN. Mr. Thornberry at the top of the fourth page says: "I must say that you are completely right." Excuse me. "... that you are completely right. People lied to us then. We didn't have any proof of that. We think that Croatia lost more than it got from the attack on the 22nd." To this, at the bottom of the page, Mr. Martic responds. That is his last sentence: "We accepted the UN to work exclusively based on the Vance Plan, which guarantees the most acceptable solutions. With this resolution the Security Council is making us leave this area or pushing us under the knives of the Croatian fascist government. I'm convinced that with your just reporting, you can influence the decisions of the Security Council." And the response to that -- by Mr. Thornberry to that is: That is hard; I would do that if that was possible." Do you see that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: What does the deputy of the UN force commanders say here? Did I understand him correctly that it is hard for him to influence the reports, the work of the Security Council of the United Nations when he's just reports [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Literally that is what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Your Honours, I do believe that it is time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How much longer are you still going to be with this witness, before we take the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, five minutes, Your Honour, another five minutes to the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Court will adjourn and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Witness, we showed you a part of this text of this document, page 4, where Mr. Martic expresses the conviction that Mr. Thornberry can influence the decisions of the Security Council with his just reports, and Mr. Thornberry says that it is hard and that if that were possible, he would do so. Let us now look at page 5 of this document. At the top of the document, in connection with this statement, Mr. Martic says: "Look at Bosnia, everyone in the world claimed that the Serbs are aggressors, but now there is shy information going around the world that the Croats and the Muslims are fighting, too, and that a classic civil war is going on. Also the world is starting to be aware that Serbs accept Croats and their soldiers in Bosnia. The western media have committed an awful crime against Serbs. They did not pass the truth to the world that the Serbs are not aggressors, that the Serbs are defending themselves." And to this, Mr. Thornberry says: "I understand you completely and I cannot understand how was it that the western media reported like that. We always also said the truth about refugees. The fact is that at this moment the Security Council has a slightly more balanced position. I think that the international community, too, is starting to get a clearer picture, but I cannot pretend to say that they have an objective position when they do not. Because of political propaganda, the international community sees all Serbs as one. We who are here see that differently. We have tried to explain all that but that is very difficult." Do you see that, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Thornberry says that it is a fact that in the council they have at least a slightly more balanced picture, what council is he referring to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: The Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the UNPROFOR had 12.000 troops deployed in the territory of the protected zones and 600 civilian observers, and then there were the European monitors and every conceivable manner of technology of this world. How do you explain the fact that in such a situation, no true reports could have been submitted to the Security Council? What is the cause of that, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: This is a very important question for me, too, so by your leave I shall be a bit more extensive. My impression and my information is such that the international community, namely the UNPROFOR forces, more specifically speaking, or precisely speaking, never implemented a balanced and equal policy, an even-handed policy towards the warring parties, and that is in keeping with Mr. Thornberry's words, in fact, when he said -- no. Delete that, when he said. What can I substantiate that with? The following. This meeting which is referred to in page 2, that was a meeting with Mr. Carl Bildt on the 3rd of July, 1995. On page 2 there is an underlined sentence. Just a minute, please. I apologise. I apologise. It is actually page 4, the first paragraph, Mr. Thornberry says: "I have to say that you're completely right. Then people lied to us. We didn't have proof of that. We think, and this is something I'm insisting on now, we think that Croatia lost more on the 22nd of January, 1993," and that is the attack on Maslenica, than it gained. Why is this essential? Because Mr. Carl Bildt used this same sentence at the meeting on the 3rd of July in Knin, and Mr. Stoltenberg was also there, when he said that in the event of a new attack by Croatia, Croatia would be gaining -- losing more than it would gain, and that is why Krajina should be calm. And this is confirmation of my thesis that the international community, i.e., the UNPROFOR forces, rather insisted more on deadening the forces of the Krajina so that no actions be undertaken in the Krajina, especially in the defensive sphere; whereas on the other hand, it allowed Croatia in breach of the Vance Plan and all other plans which required a peaceful solution to do what they did. So that during those years, five years, the -- Croatia undertook a number of military operations and attacks in the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and we had no examples of the Republic of Serbian Krajina launching any attacks against Croatian territory, and Croatian-held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Let us now look at page number 7, speaking about the position of Croats, and it says, Minister Martic, the third paragraph, or rather the penultimate and the ultimate paragraph. Mr. Martic says to Mr. Thornberry: "Regarding the positions of the Croats in the RSK, we are on our side doing everything to protect them from bullets. We have the same positions when Serbs or Croats are endangered, and as far as protection is concerned we make no distinction between them. We are doing everything to protect all people regardless of their national affiliation. "If someone insisted to leave the area of the RSK, we have nothing against it. They can go freely. It happened earlier, the Croats who expressed the desire to move out signed statements to the effect that no pressure had been exerted on them, but once in Croatia, they would say the opposite, that they had been driven out." And this continues on page 8. "The Croatian side is using this for propaganda purposes." And Mr. Martic goes on to say: "They really want to leave the Krajina, I insist that their signatures be co-signed by your side, by the United Nations, that is." And then Mr. Thornberry replies to these words of Mr. Martic's, and that is the penultimate paragraph on that page: "We can design the procedure. I now accept your statement that you are protecting people in very difficult conditions. It would be good if you could inform the public more widely about your position on this issue." Mr. Martic says: "That is what we are doing. Our public knows that. We are on our part punishing criminals, whereas Croatia is rewarding them on its territory." And then he refers to the case of the murder of the Zec family which we have also discussed here. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, a redaction? I mentioned the name of the witness. Can we have that redacted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not say the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. May we redact that part where the name of the witness is mentioned? I guess it will be mentioned in the B/C/S broadcast so can it be redacted there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Positions expressed in this conversation by Mr. Martic. Did they respond and correspond with what you knew, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes. I stated that on Friday in the same way that it is being stated here in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us take a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do propose to tender this document as a Defence Exhibit, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted as a Defence Exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Are you -- when are you finishing, Mr. Milovancevic? We are now 15 minutes since the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe in three minutes time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said five minutes before the break. We've got 15 minutes. Just move quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to invite Mr. Usher to distribute a document to the Chamber and the OTP. You spoke about the attitude towards your own population in the RSK territory. Do you know whether the MUP, Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, whether they issued any press releases on their attitude towards the entire population?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes. It was a regular occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You have before you a document dated the very end of 1991. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: This is a press release of the MUP. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it's the third paragraph from the bottom of the page. Please read it out. It's a part of a statement for the press where the Ministry of the Interior addresses the public and indicates what kind of an attitude should be adopted towards every member of the population when it comes to their ethnicity. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Could you read it out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes. "Republic of Serbian Krajina together with the MUP guarantees safety to all peoples in this territory and appeals on the citizens with the aim of protecting the lives and property of people of a different ethnicity. There is no ethnically pure countries in the world, and I believe that we have the preconditions for peaceful coexistence of the peoples of Serbian Krajina regardless of the current circumstances and developments."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who is signed as the author of that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Milan Martic, the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is there a seal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes, there is a seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Is it his signature or was it somebody on his behalf?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes, I believe a deputy of his signed on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: So Mr. Martic, as a minister, in the government, appeals to the public to be tolerant in terms of ethnicity and to be -- to have their appropriate conduct. Is it stated as so in the statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Finally, did you participate in the negotiations in Geneva on the 3rd of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the delegation of the RSK accept all conditions of the international community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Absolutely all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Who brought these conditions to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Mr. Thornberry. Wait a minute. Yeah, Thornberry presented us with those conditions. There were three conditions. First, to open the oil pipeline on the 7th of August; then until the 9th of August we can start discussions on the reopening of the railway line; and that we conduct negotiations on the Z-4 plan first in Knin and then in Zagreb on the 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Mr. Thornberry. Does the name Stoltenberg mean anything to you? So on that occasion, do you mean Mr. Thornberry or Mr. Stoltenberg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I believe that Mr. Stoltenberg attended that meeting, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You said Thornberry. Are you correcting your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes. I'm correcting my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian side accept these conditions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: No. They did not. Their position was strictly to the effect that what they insisted on was to start peaceful reintegration, as they called it, immediately, for all arms to be laid down, for Croatian laws to be accepted throughout Krajina and some other requests. When Mr. Stoltenberg offered this solution, they said we have not come here to discuss this. We take this as a negative response to our question, and we deem these negotiations concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened that evening? Did you receive any information about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: On further developments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Meeting was finished at 4.30 p.m. or maybe later, and after that, we received the information that Croatia --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I was asked by the people -- I said no, but by leaving the microphone open, I eliminated the effect of distorting the voice of the witness, and this is my mistake. I did not understand what you just asked me from the Registry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I asked you if you wanted to be redacted, if you want to ask the Judges to redact the whole part, because if you leave the microphone open, everyone can hear the voice of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to breach protective measures. Whatever is necessary to be done, I propose it be done so that the genuine voice of the witness, which left this courtroom, to be deleted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're going to have to make a proper motion, a proper request. You can't say whatever needs to be done. What is that that whatever needs to be done? You either want a redaction or you don't want a redaction. Tell us what you want, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that part of the text which was broadcast without the witness's voice being distorted, I move that it be redacted, and it was broadcast without distortion because my mic was on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So it's ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you receive that evening any information on subsequent events while you were at Geneva?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Information that came were to the effect that Mr. Babic, as the minister of foreign affairs, he was a Prime Minister of Krajina, that he had accepted the Z-4 peace plan and, in discussions with Mr. Galbraith, who was the then US ambassador, and after that, we prepared to travel back, and in the afternoon we were told by a French colonel, who was in our escort, that Croatia had attacked Krajina, which was proof enough for me that the talks in Geneva were a way for Croatia formally to respect the international community's request but in effect that they had prepared for this attack and conducted it regardless of what would transpire at Geneva,, which was a wilful breach of international obligations and the international community's efforts to resolve this conflict in a peaceful manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: How did the attack -- what was the label of that attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: That was Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've concluded my examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Milovancevic. What do you want to us do with this document that you showed the witness, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for reminding me. I move to tender this as a Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The document is admitted as an exhibit for the Defence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, my name is Mr. Black. As you may have guessed, I'm one of the members of the Prosecution team and now it's my turn to ask you questions for a while. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Now, first of all, sir, let me just briefly say what I do not intend to ask you about. You made reference in your testimony on Friday to changes in the Croatian constitution in 1991 that made Serbs a national minority rather than a constituent people. I believe you also testified that Serbs initially sought autonomy within Croatia. I don't intend to ask you any questions about those topics and it's not because the Prosecution accepts what you had to say. It's simply that we have had evidence about that in this case, and I'm going to try to focus my questions on other aspects of your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, we are back in open session now. While we are on the issue of property, it's true, isn't it, that in 1992 and 1993, there was widespread looting and seizure of property which belonged to Croats who had fled the Krajina? That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: According to reports of the Ministry of the Interior for 1992, the ministry brought 6.000 criminal reports which concerned among other things looting, concerning crimes against the Serbs, but to a great extent it refers to Croats being targets of such crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So I guess the answer to my question was yes, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: The answer is how I gave it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I can ask the question again and get you to answer it, then. It's true, isn't it, that in 1992 and 1993, there was widespread looting and seizure of property belonging to Croats who had fled the RSK? Is that right or is it wrong?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: There was looting. I cannot agree it was mass looting in the way that you presented. When it comes to the extent of the overall looting, it -- the number of such incidents was relatively low. If I may say, I don't want to contest when you say describe things that did occur, but let us be objective. There were incidents of looting, targeted against the Serbs, and many of these incidents are more numerous than those against the Croats. I'm not negating what you're saying but let us not lose sight of the fact -- I don't want us to depict -- paint a picture were there were no attacks against Croats but there were, but incidents where Serbs were victims were far more numerous than those where Croats were victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, we'll all be delighted if we can be objective here. That's what we are trying to do. And you've insisted on this now and also in your testimony on Friday, that there were more crimes against Serbs than there were against Croats. I'm right, aren't I, that certainly from the beginning of 1992 and through to August 1995, there were very few Croats living in the RSK in comparison with the number of Serbs. There were many more Serbs living there than Croats, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And so it stands to reason, doesn't it, that you might see even more crimes with Serb victims than Croat victims just because of the differences in population, right? If you were being objective.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shaking your head and finger doesn't get recorded, Witness. If you can say something, then we at least we can read it on the record here. We will not be able to see your finger wagging or your head shaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I noticed the lapse of the Prosecutor that there were more crimes against Serbs than Croats, but I wanted to indicate that I agreed with and I of course accept your rightful remark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I wanted to indicate that I agreed with what? That sentence became incomplete and then we, by a conjunction, we lumped something else that had nothing to do with the first part of the sentence. What did you agree with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know what you refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will record to you what how your answer was translated to us. Your Honour, I apologise I noticed the lapse of the Prosecutor that there were more crimes against Serbs than Croats but I wanted to indicate that I agreed with and I of course accept your rightful remark. Now, I don't know what, agreed with what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, through my gestures I wanted to indicate that I agreed that I indicated that I mentioned, noticed that the Prosecutor said that there were far more crimes against the Serbs than the Croats, rather than the opposite given the number of respective ethnic groups living in the RSK. He meant to say the opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: I'm not sure the Prosecutor told you anything, but the Prosecutor was referring to what you said yesterday or on Friday. Wasn't it the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perhaps the best thing is if I put my question again. If it wasn't clear hopefully I'll straighten it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That will be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My question is this, sir: You've told us, according to you, that there were many more Serb victims of crime than there were Croat victims of crime. And my point to you is that that wouldn't be surprising at all given the proportions of population because there were many more Serbs living in the RSK than Croats, so the fact that you -- even if we accept, as you say, that there were more victims who were Serb than Croat, that doesn't necessarily suggest that Serbs were -- in proportion to their population were more often victims than Croats. Actually, the opposite was the case; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would help by saying yes, it was right; or no, it is not right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, you were ambiguous towards the end of your statement. I seek you to be more concrete. I don't want to mislead you or give you a false impression of anybody. You meant there were more victims -- crimes against the Serbs, that's true, and Croats were less numerous and that the proportion is not that significantly different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What was ambiguous now, now that you understand the proportion? What was ambiguous? I'm not quite sure I understand what needs to be clarified now here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not sure what needs to be clarified. Mr. Prosecutor is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no. You said that the Prosecutor is ambiguous. You said: "Mr. Prosecutor, you were ambiguous." Now, what is it that is ambiguous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, what I found unclear was this statement, namely if I were to say yes, the way I saw things, that would mean that I agree that in reality there had been more or as the Prosecutor likes to put it, the de facto there had been more crimes against the Croats than against the Serbs, which is something that I cannot agree to, in relation to the general number of criminal complaints dealt with by the organs of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then if you don't agree to it you just say you don't agree with it. That's why you have a choice. You're not forced to give one answer. Mr. Prosecutor, can you put the question again and let the witness answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand the witness, I think, perhaps to have answered the first part of my question, which is -- or it was kind of agreeing with -- he already said about more -- he says that there were more crimes with Serb victims than there were with Croat victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So I'll just put the second part to you again. In proportionality to their population, Croats were, let's say, more likely to be victims of crime than were Serbs, right? Because there were far fewer Croats in the RSK than there were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this question is complete absolute speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, this witness said much earlier that there were more victims of Serb ethnicity than there were of Croats, for whatever reason. He seems to have the answer, and so I'm sure he can give us an answer here, too, as well. Unless you want us to accept what he said earlier as speculation too. I don't think we can deal with it that way. Let him answer. Let him answer and tell us. If it's speculation, let him tell us it's speculation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that no legal system, a system aspiring after regularity, can accept Mr. Prosecutor's statements to the effect that because someone is in a minority, they have more possibility --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you, Witness? I don't think it's for you to comment on the Prosecutor's questions. You just answer the question. If you're not able to answer the question, say I am not able to answer the question. If you disagree with the question, just say I disagree with the question. It's not for you to -- you're here to answer questions. Mr. Prosecutor, will you put the last part of your question to the witness again?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, again the question is: In proportion to their population, Croats in the RSK were more likely to be victims of crime than were Serbs. I don't say more likely in some kind of speculative way. I'm talking about if you compare the numbers of Croat victims to the numbers of Croats in the RSK, and then you compare the number of Serb victims to the number of Serbs in the RSK, proportionally Croats were actually more likely to be victims than were Serbs. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. This is indeed a multiple speculation. Who will commit the crime, the army, the police, the Territorial Defence? This is on a collision course with logic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Nobody is asking who committed the crime, Mr. Milovancevic. You are now bringing confusion instead of -- and causing a collision with logic, because you're now bringing in the perpetrators and that's not part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in that case, the question is wholly irrelevant because the Prosecutor has to bear in mind the points of the indictment, which says that the Territorial Defence and everyone associated with Martic persecuted the Croatian minority, and we are now dealing with the minority and majority. It is an incomprehensible question, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, you don't jump from one ground of objection to another depending on what answer you get, you know. You stay with your objection and if the Bench rules, it rules. And Mr. -- just for the record, the objection on relevance is overruled. Will you please put the question to the witness again?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And can you spare us your interventions, Mr. Milovancevic, which are intended to give an answer to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just try to put the question to you one more time, sir. And let me find it so that I can say it in just the same way so there is no confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In proportion to their population, Croats in the RSK were more likely to be victims of crime than were Serbs, weren't they? If you disagree, say so; but if you agree with me, please say so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Black, you side "likely." It sounds a little odd. We are talking about the past, so you mean it in terms of statistics?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour, thank you. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Otherwise it would sound like speculation but it is a statistical --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's exactly what I meant by "likely." Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Risk.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have an answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
