utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a simple matter. There were also Romanians, white Russians and other people in the Krajina, and their numbers were even smaller. Does this mean that they were even more in jeopardy? The numbers of the people really was of no relevance to the number of victims of crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you agree with the proposition by the Prosecution or do you disagree with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In keeping with what I've said, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, why did it have to take us something like 20 minutes to get an answer to this question? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I know we've gone a few minutes over the time for the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We will take a break and come back at 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And, Your Honours, earlier in the day there was a suggestion that we would take up a couple of issues after the break. And so what I thought I would do is try to leave five or ten minutes at the end of the day, if that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll try to remember. Last time I said that I forgot to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, at the end of the last session, we were kind of -- we getting a little bit bogged down and so I'm just going to take one minute to kind of explain the procedure with you, because I think there is some confusion and that's slowing us down. You and I aren't here today to argue. You don't need to argue with me and I'm going to try not to argue with you. My job here is to put questions to you and your job is to try answer those the best you can. And the lawyers, other people will have a chance to argue about all of this stuff at a later and appropriate time in the proceedings. So just so you understand that that's really what we are here to do is to ask and answer questions and not to argue with one another. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Before we got distracted, I think you had agreed with me to the very limited extent that you did agree that Croats did -- were -- at least on some occasions victims of property crimes in 1992 and 1993 in the RSK; is that right? Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: In particular, in Knin, around February of 1993, that was a fairly common problem; correct? Property crimes against Croat property.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I don't think that it was the case in Knin. In Knin there were the fewest such cases, i.e., problems. I don't say that there were not any, but this was where the least number of such cases happened. This referred rather more to the peripheral areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And when you refer to peripheral areas, one example would be Benkovac; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: When I say "peripheral," border areas. I'm more specifically referring to the areas which were on the line of separation between the RSK and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But you -- it's correct, isn't it, that there were also cases of such crimes against the Croat property, let's say, on the interior of the RSK, away from the lines of demarcation; that's the lines of separation, right? There were such crimes in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Such things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And one thing that made this problem more difficult for Croats is that in many cases property crimes against Croats were supported or at the very least condoned by local police commanders; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: No. That is not correct. There was an express order to the effect that the entire population had to be protected regardless of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So -- I don't think we need to look at it, it's Exhibit 728 for the assistance of the Defence and Your Honours. But if someone from UNPROFOR was to state that the seizure -- looting and seizure of Croat properties and food occurred often with the blessing of local militia commanders, and that that was -- had increased significantly in October of 1992, for instance, you would disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: No. I would not agree with that. I would disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Crimes against the property of Croats, especially if unpunished or condoned by the police as stated by the United Nations, that caused tremendous fear for Croats who were still in the Krajina, and it also sent a message to those Croats who left that they should not return to the RSK; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: It is quite certain that criminal offences do not augur for anyone including Croats as in the case referred to by you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we go into private session for a few moments, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you now about a couple of passages on the document that we have on our screen. If you could first look at paragraph 4, the second part of that, if we could scroll up a bit. And again this is in English, so I'll read out the part that I'm most interested in. According to this ECMM report it says: "Mr. Mikelic" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, my learned colleague, I apologise for interrupting you. I don't know whether Mr. Martic receives this document in his mother tongue. We have a problem if he does not. His Defence team understands the language, English language, the witness can be shown this document in English, but Mr. Martic has the right to know what kind of a document is being presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly am empathetic with the problem, but the way that things work in the trials here is that B/C/S is not a working language so when we have these kinds of original language documents in English it's often the case that we don't have a B/C/S translation. That's why counsel is required to be able to speak in English or French, one of the working languages of the Tribunal. So I apologise that there are a number of documents I'm using today that we do not have in B/C/S, and that's simply the practice to avoid translating all these things is that if it's in one of the working languages of the Tribunal we don't have necessarily a B/C/S translation. And if I -- if Your Honour - sorry to rise again - but I'll read out the pertinent passages which will be translated by the booths so hopefully that conveys all necessary information to Mr. Martic. And if not, his counsel, who understands the language, can help him with other passages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is correct, what my learned colleague says, but it seems that we have a problem with the witness as well. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I suppose the answer to that question is contained in the previous answer given by Mr. Black. Would a translation from the B/C/S booth for the witness also not be equally helpful? I know it is not the full answer but we are being told that B/C/S is not a working language of the Tribunal and that's why, and I'm looking at the rules here and looking at Rule 66, which insists on documents that must be given to the accused in his -- in a language he understands. I don't think this is one of them. Surely the very reading of Rule 66 anticipates that there will be some other documents that are not necessarily going to be in the language of the accused. Because it specifies specifically that that which must be given to him in the language that he understands. And if you look at Rule 67 and Rule 68, and Rule 68 bis, all talk of disclosures but all those disclosures are not within the meaning of Rule 66. I think we have been going on along this line, Mr. Milovancevic, and I think the Defence has also given documents that were only in English and they have read these documents. How have you solved the problem with the accused and the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it has occurred on a couple of occasions but these documents were very rare. The problem here is concerning the witness, for his benefit, his words are quoted verbatim. I'm not sure to which extent he will be able to follow the text. I'm going -- I'm talking about this general problem. I accept my learned colleague's explanation concerning the accused, but for witness, he would be put in a far more disadvantageous position if he cannot read in his mother tongue something that he purportedly stated and is being quoted as such. If he were to give a translation into B/H/S [as interpreted] he would be able to detect whether it follows his usual linguistic patterns, whether he does express himself in this way or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I think a translation is given to him in B/C/S in -- from the B/C/S booth, number 1. Number 2, I don't think the rarity of documents in English is the issue. The issue is the issue of principle, whether rare or many, if documents in English are not supposed to be used, they are not supposed to be used, irrespective of how few they may be. And the principle should apply equally to few documents as it does to many documents. But what else do you suggest we do, Mr. Milovancevic? (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've tried to do that and I'll certainly try to adopt that in the future and hopefully that will address Mr. Milovancevic's concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Black. I thought this had been done actually in this particular instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we move into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to ask you about a couple of passages from the document which is on our screen and I'll read them out to you, and again I'm -- I know that it's a bit of a problem that you don't have this in your first language, so if you have confusion or a question about what is read out to you, please let us know and we'll clarify that so that you know what the document says. And the first part I'd like to point your attention to is the second part of paragraph 4, and it's talking about something said by Mr. Mikelic and here's what the paragraph says: "Mr. Mikelic, the new Prime Minister, was quoted as saying, 'Our negotiating position is and will be territorial integrity and sovereignty of the Republic of Serb Krajina. The RSK will sooner or hater unite with the Serb republic and Montenegro into a unified state.'". And my question for you, sir, is: That was the position of Mr. Mikelic and in fact the RSK government at the time, that the RSK would sooner or later unite with Serbia and Montenegro, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: In principle, no. Why not? If I -- may I explain why not? It is beyond questioning that all of us wanted for the Serb question and issue be resolved in a just manner, and one of the options was unifying with Serbia and Montenegro and this is beyond questioning. But during a certain period, what was expressed was a possible option for the conflict to be resolved in another manner but given the pressure coming from the public, we could not state that publicly, which means that no politician in Krajina could opt for anything else although given the talks with the international community, for that position to be expressed in public before the grounds were prepared for such an expression. So we had to be mindful of these things as well. Let me be clear about it. Of course, it was beyond questioning that the desire of most people was to unify with Serbia and Montenegro. Other options being peaceful solution in accordance with the Vance Plan. There were several options open to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And I think I've understood you to say that the public position was for unification with Serbia and Montenegro sort of for political reasons, but behind the scenes there were other options being considered by the Serb leadership. Is that what I've understood -- is that -- have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought the opposite of that was the position. The public position was we go for other options according to the Vance Plan, but behind the scenes we really wanted to join with Montenegro and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Witness, perhaps you've heard -- I understood you in one way and the Bench obviously understood you in another way. Can you help us understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Resolve our differences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the way that you understood it follows from my unclear statements. This is not the case. I said that we, all of us, wanted to unify with Serbia and Montenegro, but we concurrently worked on resolving the conflict in other ways. It would be an illusion to expect at this point of time for the leadership, the political leadership of Krajina that conducted these talks, to work on just one option. It accepted other options and negotiated about them. What I wanted to state is that we could not state such options publicly, which does not mean that we wanted to circumvent the Vance Plan. We wanted to enforce that plan to the benefit, peacefully to the benefit of all the peoples in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which is this option that you were not prepared to state publicly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are the options that were linked to talks with Croatia about the pipeline, the roads, establishing of other forms of cooperation, and we state -- we meant that time will show which option would be the best one. Requesting that Republic of Serbian Krajina unilaterally to be annexed to Serbia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are introducing pipelines now and roads. The question was there were -- the options that we are talking about are two here: Either to work on the Vance Plan, according to the proposals of the Vance Plan, or to unite with Serbia and Montenegro. Which of these two was the option that the Krajina officials were not prepared to state publicly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The option was to work in accordance with the Vance Plan. In accordance with the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And which was not supposed to be mentioned publicly? Can you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What could not be mentioned publicly is that the issue of the Republic of Serbian Krajina can be resolved in no other way but through unification with Serbia and Montenegro because majority of the people expected that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's how I understood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, the position vis-a-vis the international community was also always that the RSK insisted on a separate state as any solution to the conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: That was one of the most frequently referred to solutions. It was not the sole one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, it was one -- it was the only one acceptable, really, to the RSK leadership; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: I just said something different. It was just one of the solutions, the most frequent one but it wasn't the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps we will come back to that later on in my questions. Let me ask you about one other part of this document while it's on our screen and it's in paragraph 5. In there, this document says the following. It says: "Mr. Babic later in a statement said that all members of the government must persist in achieving the sovereignty of the RSK and the right of the Serb people to self-determination and unification with other parts of the Serb people." And that's another reference to this same idea of unification; correct? Unification with Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I didn't hear an interpretation but I see it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I got it. Thank you. Your Honours, could this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number 970.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, while we are on this issue of joining Serb lands into one state, that was Milan Martic's position at the time also, wasn't it, both publicly and privately, he was a proponent of this idea of unifying Serb lands into one state.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And for example, during the presidential elections in I guess December of 1993 and January of 1994, Martic said that if he won the election, he would "speed up the process of unification," and that he would "pass on the baton to our all Serbian leader Slobodan Milosevic." You remember him saying those types of things about unification with Serbia and Montenegro, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS MM-117
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember that was literally so, but that he did utter such a wish and that that was an objective, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could we move back into private session now for a while, please, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could the Chamber please move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 17th day of October, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
